provenance.note: 14 Acid-base balance.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Plasma pH 7.37-7.43; pH = -log [H⁺].
CO₂ is volatile (lungs); fixed acids (lactate, ketones, phosphoric, sulphuric) go through the kidneys.
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂).
Main extracellular buffer: bicarbonate; main red-cell buffer: haemoglobin.
Phosphate buffer matters most in urine.
Lungs: fast; kidneys: slow but powerful and lasting.
Bicarbonate excreted above 28 mmol/L.
Renal H⁺: 1/3 titratable acidity, 2/3 ammonium; each H⁺ regenerates one HCO₃⁻.
Acidosis ↔ hyperkalaemia (H⁺/K⁺ exchange).
Blood gases: anaerobic heparinised syringe, on ice, within 1 h.
PaCO₂ 37-43 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22-26 mmol/L; PaO₂ 75-100 mmHg.
Anion gap = (Na + K) - (Cl + HCO₃) = 12 ± 2.

deeper.title: Why bicarbonate is the best buffer despite its pKa of 6.1
deeper.html:
A pKa of 6.1 is a full unit below blood pH, which would make a closed buffer weak. But the bicarbonate system is open: the lungs remove CO₂ and the kidneys adjust bicarbonate, so neither side of the pair runs out. That dual control makes it the most effective extracellular buffer, as the lecture explains.

Source: the lecture's bicarbonate buffer slide.

deeper.title: Why compensation never overshoots
deeper.html:
Compensation is driven by the pH error itself. As pH returns toward normal, the stimulus fades, so the compensating change slows before pH is fully corrected. A pH on the opposite side of 7.40 therefore points to a second, mixed disorder rather than 'over-compensation'.

Source: the lecture's disorder table.

deeper.title: Why adrenaline is given in anaphylaxis
deeper.html:
Adrenaline hits alpha-1 receptors, constricting vessels and raising blood pressure, and beta-2 receptors, opening the bronchi. In anaphylaxis the patient has dangerously low blood pressure and narrowed airways at once, so one drug reverses both.

Source: the lecture's receptor actions and conclusion slides.

provenance.note: 11 Calcium phosphate balance.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Ca: 99% in bone; P: 85% in bone.
Serum Ca: 50% diffusible (45% ionised), 50% protein-bound (80% albumin).
Ca absorbed mainly in the duodenum; P in the jejunum-ileum.
Active Ca absorption is calcitriol-dependent and saturable; passive above ~600 mg/day.
Kidney reabsorbs 95% of filtered Ca and 90% of filtered P.
PTH: Ca↑ P↓; calcitonin: Ca↓ P↓; calcitriol: Ca↑ P↑.
PTH: 84 amino acids, active N-terminal fragment.
Calcitonin comes from thyroid parafollicular cells.
Calcaemia 85-105 mg/L (2.25-2.60 mmol/L); no EDTA, citrate, oxalate.
Corrected Ca = measured + (40 - albumin)/40.
Phosphataemia: adult 30-40 mg/L, child 40-60 mg/L.

deeper.title: Why low albumin fakes hypocalcaemia
deeper.html:
Half of serum calcium rides on proteins, mostly albumin, but only the ionised fraction acts on cells. When albumin falls, bound calcium falls and total calcium looks low, while ionised calcium can be perfectly normal. The correction formula adds back 0.025 mmol/L for each g/L of missing albumin.

Source: the lecture's Purfitt formula slide.

deeper.title: Why PTH moves calcium and phosphate in opposite directions
deeper.html:
Releasing calcium from bone also releases phosphate, and a high product of the two would precipitate in tissues. PTH solves this by making the kidney excrete phosphate while it retains calcium, so blood calcium rises without phosphate following.

Source: the lecture's parathyroid hormone slide.

hs-troponin rises at 2 h, conventional 4 h; peak 14 h.
cTnI 75 to 140 h; cTnT over 10 days.
Troponin C not cardiac-specific.
BNP/NT-proBNP: chronic heart failure; NT-proBNP distorted in renal failure.
CRP peaks 48 to 72 h; persistent low CRP = CV risk.

deeper.title: Why a single normal troponin is not enough
deeper.html:
Troponin takes 2 to 4 hours to rise after the start of the pain. A patient who arrives within an hour may have a normal first result while an infarction is developing, which is why troponin is repeated a few hours later before ruling out a heart attack.

Source: the lecture's troponin kinetics slides.

exam_points: Liver flow 75 percent portal.
ALT liver-specific; AST also heart, muscle.
Transaminases very high in acute hepatitis.
Cholestasis: ALP and GGT rise together.
Isolated GGT: chronic alcoholism.
Bilirubin 3.4 to 17.1; jaundice eyes above 30, skin above 50 µmol/L.
Protect bilirubin from light.
Albumin 35 to 50 g/L; PT +3 s = bleeding risk.
AFP: HCC; ceruloplasmin low: Wilson's.

deeper.title: Why the prothrombin time is the best quick test of liver function
deeper.html:
Clotting factors are made by the liver and several have half-lives of hours, so the prothrombin time lengthens within a day of acute liver failure, long before albumin (half-life about three weeks) falls. If giving vitamin K corrects it, the problem was cholestasis; if not, the liver itself is failing.

Source: the lecture's coagulation factor slides, with standard physiology.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Insulin: beta cells; only hypoglycaemic hormone.
A chain 21, B chain 30; gene chromosome 11.
Proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide.
Glucose → ATP → K+ channels close → Ca2+ entry → release.
Activates glycogenesis, glycolysis, lipogenesis.
Inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis.
HbA1c every 2 to 3 months; fructosamine if haemoglobinopathy.

deeper.title: Why C-peptide tells you if insulin is the patient's own
deeper.html:
The beta cell releases insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts, but injected insulin contains no C-peptide. So a hypoglycaemic patient with high insulin but low C-peptide has been given insulin, while high levels of both point to the patient's own beta cells, as in an insulinoma.

Source: the lecture's proinsulin cleavage slide, with standard clinical reasoning.

provenance.note: 12 Iron balance.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Body iron ≈ 4 g; 60% in haemoglobin; 35% in stores.
Haem iron Fe²⁺; non-haem Fe³⁺.
Needs: 1 mg/day men, 2 mg/day women, up to 10 mg/day late pregnancy.
Absorption: duodenum, ~10% of intake; vitamin C helps.
Transferrin binds 2 Fe³⁺, ~1/3 saturated; rises when stores fall.
TIBC = transferrin × 25; TS = iron / (25 × transferrin) × 100.
Ferritin reflects stores; first-line test for deficiency.
Ferritin < 30 µg/L + anaemia = iron deficiency anaemia.
WHO anaemia: Hb < 120 g/L women, < 130 g/L men.
Hepcidin blocks iron exit; low in HFE haemochromatosis.
Haemochromatosis screening: TS > 45%.
sTfR rises in deficiency and helps in inflammation.

deeper.title: Why ferritin misleads in inflammation
deeper.html:
Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein: inflammation raises it whatever the stores. A patient with chronic inflammation and genuinely empty stores can therefore show a normal ferritin. The soluble transferrin receptor is not raised by inflammation but rises when erythroblasts are iron-hungry, so it reveals the deficiency hidden behind the inflammation.

Source: the lecture's conclusion on sTfR.

deeper.title: Why HFE mutations overload the liver, heart and pancreas
deeper.html:
Without enough hepcidin, enterocytes keep exporting iron even when the body is full. Transferrin saturates, and the surplus circulates as non-transferrin-bound iron that the liver, heart and pancreas take up avidly. That is why haemochromatosis brings cirrhosis, heart failure and diabetes.

Source: the lecture's HFE protein slide.

provenance.note: 10 Exploration of a lipid anomaly.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Lipoprotein core: TG and cholesterol esters; shell: phospholipids, free cholesterol, apoproteins.
Cholesterol: 1/3 dietary, 2/3 hepatic.
Apo AI activates LCAT; LDL carries apo B100.
Chylomicrons: most TG, largest, least dense. HDL: densest, smallest.
LPL hydrolyses TG of chylomicrons and VLDL.
VLDL → IDL → LDL (hepatic lipase).
HDL + LCAT: reverse cholesterol transport (anti-atherogenic).
Fast 12 h; wait 3-4 months after an MI.
Lactescent serum = chylomicrons; opalescent = VLDL/IDL.
Friedewald: LDL = TC - HDL - TG/5 (g/L), valid if TG < 3.5 g/L.
LDL target < 2.6 mmol/L if risk factors, < 4 without.
Apo B/apo AI ratio: best measure of atherogenic risk.

deeper.title: Why Friedewald fails when triglycerides are high
deeper.html:
The formula estimates VLDL cholesterol as a fixed fraction of triglycerides (TG/5 in g/L). When triglycerides are very high, chylomicrons and remnants appear with a different cholesterol/TG ratio, the estimate breaks down, and the calculated LDL becomes wrong. That is why LDL must be measured directly above 3.5 g/L.

Source: the lecture's reference values slide.

deeper.title: Why the serum's appearance is informative
deeper.html:
Particles scatter light in proportion to their size. Huge chylomicrons make serum milky and, being light, float up as a creamy layer on standing; smaller VLDL make it uniformly cloudy; LDL and HDL are too small to affect clarity. A clear serum therefore does not rule out high LDL cholesterol.

Source: the lecture's serum appearance slide.

deeper.title: Why a potassium of 6.5 might be a lab artefact
deeper.html:
Red cells hold most of the body's potassium. If a sample is haemolysed by a tight tourniquet or a small needle, or sits for hours before analysis, potassium leaks out and the result looks dangerously high. Before treating hyperkalaemia in a well patient, check whether the sample was haemolysed or delayed.

Source: the lecture's haemolysis and storage slides.

deeper.title: Why a normal creatinine can hide kidney disease
deeper.html:
Creatinine reflects muscle mass as well as filtration. An elderly, thin woman makes little creatinine, so her level can look normal while her GFR has already fallen by half. That is why estimated GFR formulas adjust for age and sex, and why cystatin C helps in people with low muscle mass.

Source: the lecture's creatinine and cystatin C slides.

provenance.note: 9 Serum protein electrophoresis.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Five fractions: albumin, α1, α2, β, γ.
Alkaline buffer pH 8.2-8.6: all proteins negative, migrate to the anode.
Albumin migrates fastest; the liver makes all but gamma globulins.
Use serum (dry tube), not plasma: fibrinogen gives a false band.
Haemolysis adds a haemoglobin band (splits α2).
Normal A/G ratio 1.2 to 1.8.
Inflammation: α1 and α2 up.
Nephrotic syndrome: albumin down, α2 up.
Cirrhosis: beta-gamma block (polyclonal IgA).
Monoclonal spike → immunofixation (myeloma vs Waldenström).
PEP orients the diagnosis; it does not confirm it.

deeper.title: Why albumin runs furthest
deeper.html:
At pH 8.6 albumin carries a large net negative charge for its size, so the electric field pulls it hardest toward the anode. Immunoglobulins have isoelectric points close to neutral and carry little charge at that pH, so they barely move and stay near the application point. That is why the order runs albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, gamma.

Source: the lecture's principle slides.

deeper.title: Why a narrow spike is worrying and a dome is not
deeper.html:
Each plasma-cell clone makes one exact immunoglobulin, with one charge and one migration speed, so a single clone expanding gives a sharp, narrow peak. An infection activates many clones at once, each with slightly different antibodies, which spread across the gamma zone as a broad dome. A spike therefore points to one abnormal clone, as in myeloma, and needs immunofixation.

Source: the lecture's gamma-globulin variation slides.

deeper.title: Why a blocked enzyme makes girls look male
deeper.html:
In 21-hydroxylase deficiency the adrenal cannot finish cortisol. With no cortisol, the pituitary keeps pushing ACTH, which drives the whole pathway harder. Precursors pile up before the block and spill into the one route still open, the androgen pathway, flooding the fetus with androgens.

Source: the lecture's 21-hydroxylase deficiency slides.

provenance.note: 2 Thyroid hormones.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Lecture 02, Prof. Nabiha Kamal, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: The thyroid is vital: no life without thyroid hormones.
Iodine from food; iodide captured by active transport; oxidised by TPO.
TPO: oxidation, iodination (MIT, DIT) and coupling (DIT+DIT = T4, DIT+MIT = T3).
Lysosomal enzymes free the hormones; deiodinase recycles iodine from MIT/DIT.
Secreted: T4 (90%), T3, reverse T3 (inactive). Only T3 and T4 act.
Only the free fraction is active; FT4 and FT3 matter in diagnosis.
TBG (liver) carries T4 most; TBPA mainly T3; albumin non-specific.
Most T3 is made peripherally from T4 by deiodinase; T3 is 10x more active.
T3 receptors in the cytoplasm and the nucleus.
TRH → TSH → T4; T4 gives negative feedback. TSH: common alpha, specific beta chain.
Catabolism: conjugation, TRIAC/TETRAC, deiodination (80% of T4).
Actions: heat, glycolysis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis; synergy with GH; more adrenergic receptors.
Graves: anti-TSH receptor antibodies. Hashimoto: anti-thyroglobulin, anti-TPO.
Amiodarone: check before, then every 6 months.
FT4 = positive diagnosis; TSHus = central versus peripheral.
Half-life T3 1 day, T4 1 week: treat with T4 once daily.

deeper.title: Reading FT4 and TSH together
deeper.html:
Think of the feedback loop. If the thyroid itself fails (peripheral), FT4 falls and the healthy pituitary pushes TSH up. If the pituitary or hypothalamus fails (central), both FT4 and TSH are low. In peripheral hyperthyroidism (Graves'), high FT4 silences the pituitary, so TSH is very low. The tutorial cases are all built on this logic, and a TRH test then tells a pituitary cause (TSH does not rise) from a hypothalamic one (TSH rises).

Source: the lecture's regulation and exploration slides; Tutorial 2 (2025-2026).

deeper.title: Why hypothyroidism raises cholesterol
deeper.html:
Tutorial 2 explains it: with less thyroid hormone, basal metabolism slows and acetyl-CoA is no longer used as much in the Krebs cycle. The excess acetyl-CoA is diverted to cholesterol synthesis, so a patient with hypothyroidism can present with hypercholesterolaemia.

Source: Tutorial 2, clinical case 1.

provenance.note: 13 Hydro-electrolytic balance.pdf (Clinical Biochemistry, Prof. Nabiha Kamal)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Water = 60% of body weight (50% women, 75% infants).
Intracellular 28 L; interstitial 12 L; plasma 3 L.
Intake = output = 2.5 L/day; urine 1.5 L.
Plasma: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ dominate. Cells: K⁺ and phosphates dominate.
Interstitial fluid = plasma without proteins (Donnan).
K⁺ > 6.5 mmol/L is life-threatening.
Haemolysis and delay raise potassium; EDTA falsifies K⁺, Na-heparin Na⁺.
Hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperproteinaemia give false hyponatraemia.
Osmolality = (Na + K) × 2 + urea + glucose = 280-300 mOsm/kg.
ADH retains water; aldosterone retains Na⁺ and water; ANF excretes them.
Diabetes insipidus → intracellular dehydration.

deeper.title: Why sodium tracks osmolality
deeper.html:
Sodium and its accompanying anions make up almost all the osmotically active particles outside cells, which is why the osmolality formula starts with (Na + K) × 2. Because water moves freely across cell membranes, a low sodium means cells swell and a high sodium means they shrink: the brain feels this first, causing confusion and seizures.

Source: the lecture's osmolality slide.

deeper.title: Why a haemolysed sample shows false hyperkalaemia
deeper.html:
Red cells hold about 30 times more potassium than plasma. Rupturing even a few of them during a difficult draw, or letting the tube wait too long, releases enough potassium to raise the measured value. The patient's real potassium may be normal, so a high result from a haemolysed sample must be repeated.

Source: the lecture's pre-analytical conditions slide.
